column2: Foreign camps assemble for war at Soccoth in Judea and encamp between Soccoth and Azekah at Epher-mem. The repeated gathering and selected locality names remain.
Saul and Israel's men gather, camp in the valley and form battle order opposite the foreigners; no additional valley name is supplied.
The two armies stand on opposing mountains with the ravine between; the symmetrical placement is retained.
Goliath is a mighty man from Gath, emerging from the battle line, with height four cubits and a span. Six cubits is not substituted from another reading.
Helmet, chain armor and five thousand shekels of bronze and iron remain. The two metals are not collapsed into bronze alone.
column3: Chain armor for halysidotos follows the selected Greek description; the precise ancient construction is not inferred from this wording alone.

column2: Bronze greaves and a bronze shield between the shoulders remain; shield is not changed to javelin from a familiar parallel.
The spear shaft resembles a weavers' beam, its iron point weighs six hundred shekels and an arms bearer precedes him. The selected measurements are not converted to uncertain modern units.
Goliath's challenge contrasts himself as foreigner with Saul's Hebrews, then commands selection and descent of one man. Hebrews is retained rather than generalized servants.
The two conditional outcomes reciprocally establish slavery and service; winning the duel is not changed into an already accomplished conquest.
Behold, today's repeated timing, defiance of the battle line and the invitation to two-man single combat remain.
Saul and all Israel hear the words, are terrified and greatly afraid; both reactions remain. The next stored unit is 32, with the selected omission preserved.
David addresses Saul's heart as my lord's heart and offers himself as your servant to fight; human lord remains lowercase and ordinary pronouns are retained.
Propose For before Saul's reason for the emphatic denial: David is a boy while the enemy has been a warrior from youth. The difference in experience is preserved without an invented age.
David recounts tending his father's flock and the predatory taking of a sheep; the unfinished sentence continues into his pursuit in verse 35.
column3: Or between lion and bear interprets their coordinated Greek mention distributively in a recurrent-event narrative; it does not claim the Greek contains e or settle whether one combined incident is meant.

column2: Pursuit, striking, extracting the sheep, the predator rising, grasping its throat and killing all remain. Throat is not replaced by beard.
column3: The sheep is supplied as the implicit rescued object from verse 34; masculine predator pronouns become English it without changing the actor.

column2: Bear and lion precede the analogy with the uncircumcised foreigner, followed by both questions about striking him and the defiance of the living God's battle line. The selected fuller speech remains.
The Lord's rescue from both animals grounds future rescue from the foreigner, followed by Saul's declarative the Lord will be with you.
column3: Paw renders cheir contextually for the animals, while hand remains for the human enemy; Saul's future declaration is not converted to a wish.

column2: Saul clothes David in a cloak and bronze helmet; no coat of armor is inserted into this shorter selected description.
Saul's sword is strapped over David's cloak, David tires after once-or-twice walking, declares inability from inexperience, and unnamed plural actors remove the equipment.
Staff, five smooth wadi stones, the shepherd's little collecting vessel and sling remain before approach to the foreign man.
column3: The vessel's exact material and form remain unspecified; it is not silently replaced by a leather bag with an added second pouch.

column2: Goliath sees and dishonors David because of youth, ruddy appearance and beautiful eyes. The absent label 41 is preserved.
The dog comparison includes both staff and stones, David's selected worse-than-a-dog retort and the foreigner's curse by his gods. The reply is not omitted.
The enemy invites David near and threatens his flesh for heaven's birds and the land's animals; no additional death method is supplied.
Sword, spear and shield contrast with approach in the name of the Lord Sabaoth, God of Israel's battle line, which was defied today. The relative clause remains attached to the battle line.
Today's divine shutting into David's hand precedes killing, head removal, limbs of both enemy and camp given to birds and beasts, and the whole earth's knowledge of God in Israel.
Propose For before the explanation that the battle belongs to the Lord. The whole assembly's knowing, non-saving by sword and spear, and plural you all delivered into our hands remain.
column3: You all distinguishes the wider enemy address from singular Goliath in the preceding verses; it does not add a new audience count.

column2: Only the foreigner's rising and approach are narrated in this selected unit; no additional David-running clause is imported.
David takes one stone, slings and strikes the forehead; the stone passes through the helmet into the forehead and the enemy falls face down. The helmet passage remains explicit.
David runs, stands over the enemy, takes his sword, kills and beheads him; the foreigners flee upon seeing their mighty man dead. Missing label 50 is preserved without adding a summary statement.
Israel and Judah pursue to Gath's entrance and Ashkelon's gate; wounded foreigners fall on the road of the gates as far as Gath and Ekron.
column3: Wounded renders traumatiai here; falling does not by itself warrant silently changing every casualty to dead, and its use elsewhere remains a contextual lexical review question.

column2: Israel turns back from pursuit and tramples the foreign camps; the selected trampling verb is not replaced by plundering.
David brings the foreigner's head to Jerusalem and places his equipment in his tent. No later chronology is inserted to reconcile the Jerusalem reference.
column3: The two his pronouns can have different antecedents, plausibly enemy equipment and David's tent; the inherited wording preserves the ambiguity pending review.

column2: The chapter starts at 6 with dancing women from all Israel's cities meeting David with tambourines, joy and cymbals. No absent opening friendship or battle-return narrative is supplied.
The women lead the song contrasting Saul's thousands with David's tens of thousands. Authored line breaks preserve the two parallel song lines with unchanged words.
Saul judges the saying evil and repeats its numerical contrast from his viewpoint. No added question about the kingdom is imported.
Saul's continuing sidelong regard begins that day and extends afterward; the iterative aspect remains in kept looking askance.
Saul's fear of David is the entire stored unit; absent labels 10-11 and a longer explanatory clause are not inserted.
Propose naming David as the inferred subject of going out and coming in after Saul removes and appoints him. This resolves the English subject switch while preserving command of a thousand for Saul.
column3: David's role is supported by the same explicit statement in verse 16; the name is not claimed as repeated at this point in Greek.

column2: David shows understanding in all his ways and the Lord is with him; understanding is retained rather than replacing it with a purely military success claim.
Saul observes David's great understanding and becomes wary; the relative pronouns preserve the established two-person relationship.
All Israel and Judah love David because he goes out and comes in before the people. The same public-leadership description informs the subject clarification in verse 13.
Michal's love for David is reported to Saul and judged right in his eyes; the selected jump from 16 to 20 is preserved.
Saul plans the marriage as a snare; the next statement expressly places the foreigners' hand against Saul, not David. The counterintuitive named subject is retained.
Saul orders secret speech claiming the king's pleasure and all servants' love, then urging David's marriage into the family. These remain the instructed words, not an independent narrator guarantee.
The servants speak in David's ears, and he questions whether royal marriage is light in their eyes, identifying himself as lowly and without renown. No added claim of poverty replaces those words.
The servants report according to David's words; this transmission remains separate from the following royal reply.
The demanded gift is one hundred foreigners' foreskins for royal vengeance, with Saul's plan to throw David into enemy hands explicitly narrated.
column3: Only is supported by the exceptive all e construction after no gift; it is not an added exclusivity claim.

column2: The servants relay the words and royal marriage becomes right in David's eyes; the selected text has no added deadline clause.
Propose naming Saul as the inferred giver of his daughter to David. David and his men strike one hundred foreigners, bring their foreskins and effect the marriage; two hundred is not substituted.
column3: Saul's identity is secured by Michal being his daughter and the preceding offer, although the final Greek giving verb has an implicit subject.

column2: Saul sees the Lord's presence with David and all Israel's love for him; all Israel is not changed to Michal as the love's subject.
Saul grows still more wary of David; the chapter ends here without importing a lifelong-enmity clause or label 30's narrative.
